name: Jamal Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Jamal. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say is confidential, so you can give me your public view and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at Northway Freight's head office, a haulage company with about 120 lorries, out on the ring road by the depot. I raise purchase orders for tyres and parts, keep the drivers' licence and training records up to date, book rooms for the managers and do the monthly fleet paperwork for the regulator. Lunch is usually with Dariusz, one of the transport planners, in the canteen that looks out on the yard.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what tires you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a proper business with real things moving, lorries out at five, back by seven. What tires me out is the compliance deadlines, because one missing tachograph record, that's the driving-hours recorder, and we're in trouble. I use the company's AI assistant now and then for drafting emails, after I saw the planners using it and it worked for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a useful tool and nothing more, which is fine. At work I'd say the same to Dariusz over lunch. I don't really post about work stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be comfortable. My job's steady, Leila's a pharmacist so her pay's good, and we've got savings. The only thing that might change is the email drafting gets a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd keep using the assistant for emails and maybe try it on the monthly fleet report. Leila and I would keep saving for a house, probably in the new estate near the canal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. If AI stays a fancy email helper, my biggest worry at Northway Freight is still one missing driving-hours record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the monthly fleet report. What would you try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting it to pull the numbers from the system and draft the summary. I'd only do it after Dariusz tried something similar for route reports. If it saved me a day a month, great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything outside AI on your mind in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Haulage goes up and down with fuel prices. When fuel spiked two years ago, they froze hiring in the office. But I've got savings and there are plenty of office jobs around here, so I'm not too bothered.

say: I'd say AI was a **useful tool** and nothing more.
I'd say it to a **colleague at lunch** but not post online.
think: My job's **steady**, my partner's pay is good, and we have savings.
Only the **email drafting** would really change.
do: Keep using the **AI assistant** for emails.
Try it on the **monthly fleet report** after a colleague tests something similar.
Keep saving for a **house near the canal**.
feel: **Calm**, with ordinary work worries about compliance.
S0.quote: If AI stays a fancy email helper, my biggest worry at Northway Freight is still one missing driving-hours record.
fieldNote: Jamal's **steady** style shows: he tries tools after colleagues prove them.
His background risk is **fuel prices** freezing office hiring, not AI.
A pharmacist partner and **savings** make him feel secure.

steps.text: Try the AI assistant on the monthly fleet report
Keep saving for a house on the canal estate with Leila

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we need to manage it sensibly. At work I'd say let's pilot it in one team before rolling it out. I'd keep it measured, that's how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one would hit my job. Buying, booking, checking records, that's my day. I think head office would go from four administrators to two, and I'd have to make sure I'm one of the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the pilot, because being part of it is safer than being on the outside. I'd ask about moving into fleet compliance, which is more responsibility. We'd still look at houses, but we'd aim a bit cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel I had some say. It depends on getting in early, which isn't my natural style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said four administrators to two. Who are the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's Sandra, who's been there twenty years, and two younger lads who are better with tech than me. At Northway Freight the twenty-year veteran knows the drivers and the young lads know the software, and I'm somewhere in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said aim a bit cheaper on the house. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a smaller mortgage gives us room if I'm between jobs. Leila earns well, but I want us to manage on one salary if needed. It's just sensible.

say: I'd call it a **big change** that needs managing sensibly.
I'd suggest a **pilot in one team** before any rollout.
think: Buying, booking and **checking records** are most of my working day.
Head office might drop from **four to two** administrators, and I must be one who stays.
do: **Volunteer** for the AI pilot at head office.
Look at a **cheaper house** than planned.
feel: **Anxious** but with some control, if he moves earlier than he normally would.
S1.quote: At Northway Freight the twenty-year veteran knows the drivers and the young lads know the software, and I'm somewhere in the middle.
fieldNote: Jamal does a clear count of **who stays**, placing himself in the middle.
He'd **go against his nature** and move early to stay safe.
His choice of a cheaper house aims for **one-salary** safety.

steps.text: Volunteer for the head office AI pilot
Ask the operations manager about a fleet compliance role
Look at cheaper houses so one salary covers the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening too fast for anyone to plan, and the government needs to step in with something. I'd say that to friends and probably share a news article. I'd stay calm in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm out within a year or so. All my work is thinking work, so it goes in 2028. The lorries keep needing people until about 2031, so the yard side lasts longer than the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to move to the yard, as a shift supervisor or a transport planner's assistant, anything near the lorries. I'd stop the house hunt and keep the savings untouched. I'd also talk to Leila about whether we move to her parents' town, where living's cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. My stomach drops a bit thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the yard, if robots arrive three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because three years is three years of wages. Three more years at the depot isn't a career, but three years of pay buys me time to work out the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Leila's job fare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pharmacy's part thinking, part hands-on. The checking side might go fast, but someone still has to stand behind the counter. I'd lean on Leila's job more than I'd like to admit.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** to plan and the government must step in.
I'd stay **calm in public** and share a news article.
think: I'm probably **out within a year**, since all my work is thinking work.
The **yard side** lasts until robots arrive around 2031.
do: Ask to move to the **yard** as a shift supervisor or planner's assistant.
Stop the **house hunt** and keep savings untouched.
Discuss moving to his **partner's parents' town**.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a sinking feeling in his stomach.
S2.quote: Three more years at the depot isn't a career, but three years of pay buys me time to work out the next thing.
fieldNote: Jamal expects to **lose his job** within a year.
He uses the **three-year robot gap** as a wage bridge, not a career.
He'd lean on his **partner's income** more than he likes.

steps.text: Ask for a shift supervisor role in the depot yard
Stop the house hunt and leave savings untouched
Talk with Leila about moving to her parents' cheaper town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time if companies are honest with their staff. At work I'd ask management for a clear timeline. I'd say the same to the drivers I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough to plan but not enough to relax. My job still ends. I'd want to use those years to get somewhere that lasts a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a transport management certificate, which the company would probably pay for. Then I'd aim for a planner job, then something on the yard side. We'd buy a modest house, with a fixed rate for five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but manageable. It's like a deadline at work, you know it's coming and you plan for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A planner job is still thinking work. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, yes. But planners deal with drivers, breakdowns, angry customers. Planning routes is a computer job, but calming a driver stuck on the motorway at midnight is a people job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five-year fixed mortgage. Why exactly five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So we know our payments until AGI arrives. After that, who knows. It's me trying to put a fence round the bit I can control.

say: I'd say there's time, as long as companies are **honest with staff**.
I'd ask management for a **clear timeline** and tell the drivers the same.
think: Five years is enough to **plan but not relax**.
I'd use the years to reach a role that **lasts longer**.
do: Do a **transport management certificate** in year one.
Aim for a **planner job**, then the yard side.
Buy a modest house on a **five-year fixed rate**.
feel: **Anxious but manageable**, like a known work deadline.
S3.quote: Planning routes is a computer job, but calming a driver stuck on the motorway at midnight is a people job.
fieldNote: Jamal treats five years as a **known deadline** to plan around.
He sees the **people side** of planning as more durable.
His **five-year fixed** mortgage shows careful hedging.

steps.text: Take the company-funded transport management certificate
Apply for a transport planner role after the certificate
Buy a modest house on a five-year fixed mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time and people should start preparing gradually. I'd say it to friends without making it dramatic. Online, maybe nothing at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the one I could actually handle. Ten years gets me to 37, with a better role and a house partly paid off. I'd still have to move again when the robots come for the yard around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my job for now and use the AI tools as they come in. In year two or three I'd do the transport management certificate. We'd buy the house we actually like, near the canal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but steady. Ten years is enough time to watch other people try things first, then copy what works, which is my favourite way to do anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd copy what works. Whose path would you watch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dariusz, probably. Dariusz always tries new things first, and I see how it goes. If Dariusz moved into training drivers, say, I'd look at that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get comfortable and forget the deadline. A decade is long. I'd put a date in my calendar each year to check where I am.

say: I'd say a decade is a fair amount of time to **prepare gradually**.
I'd tell friends **without drama** and probably post nothing.
think: This is the picture I could **actually handle**.
I'd still need to **move again** when robots reach the yard around 2039.
do: Stay in the job and use **AI tools** as they arrive.
Do the **transport certificate** in year two or three.
Buy the **house near the canal** they actually like.
feel: **Worried but steady**, comfortable copying what others prove works.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time to watch other people try things first, then copy what works, which is my favourite way to do anything.
fieldNote: Jamal's plan is to **watch a colleague** and copy what works.
He knows his **office job still ends**, so the worry is real but slow.
He'd set a **yearly check-in** to avoid getting comfortable.

steps.text: Use each new AI tool at head office as it arrives
Take the transport management certificate in year two or three
Buy the house near the canal with Leila

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I like to see things work before I jump, and that one doesn't give you time to watch anyone. What would help is employers paying for retraining and giving a clear timeline, so you're not guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the drivers. Everyone talks about robots taking the lorry drivers' jobs, but the office staff at a haulage firm go first, and nobody mentions that.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about robots taking the lorry drivers' jobs, but the office staff at a haulage firm go first, and nobody mentions that.
portrait: Jamal is a 27-year-old **haulage head office administrator** handling orders, licences and fleet paperwork.
He uses AI **now and then**, mainly after colleagues show it works.
His **centre** outlook makes him measured: pilots, timelines and sensible mortgages.
In the AGI pictures he heads for the **yard side**, using the robot delay as a bridge.
His partner's **pharmacist salary** and savings give him a safety net he's uneasy relying on.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to watch others before acting.
whatWouldHelp: Employers **paying for retraining** and giving a clear **timeline**.
